name: Judicial reasoning

subjectOf.text: Judge Baer's dismissal of the Porsche complaint reaches the correct result under Morrison, but parts of his reasoning require further refinement.
subjectOf.abstract: In sum, Judge Baer's holding is correct under Morrison, but some of the reasoning needs further refinement.
subjectOf.citation: Kaal and Painter, The Aftermath of Morrison v. National Australia Bank and Elliott Associates v. Porsche (2011). SSRN: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1765901
scope_conditions: security-based swap agreements referencing foreign traded stock

subjectOf.text: The Shenzhen courts illustrate a workable three step human-in-the-loop design for generative judicial AI: the judge decides first, the LLM generates the supporting reasoning, and the judge then revises that output to finalize the judgment.
subjectOf.abstract: A notable case study from Shenzhen, China, illustrates a three-step interaction pattern: judges make initial decisions, LLMs generate reasoning based on these decisions, and judges revise the output to finalize judgments.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Morgan A. Gray, The Evolving Role of Artificial Intelligence in Law (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5541658
scope_conditions: Chinese courts using LLMs to draft judicial opinions

subjectOf.text: Even as LLMs for judicial reasoning become more sophisticated, their inability to replicate empathy and social responsiveness will confine them to supportive rather than decisional functions.
subjectOf.abstract: However, AI's inability to replicate empathy and social responsiveness will limit its role to supportive functions.
subjectOf.citation: Wulf A. Kaal, Morgan A. Gray, The Evolving Role of Artificial Intelligence in Law (2025). SSRN: https://ssrn.com/abstract=5541658
scope_conditions: judicial reasoning and opinion drafting applications
